title: Resilient Societies and Crisis Response Research Workshop
subtitle: Integrating Data, Technology, and Social Perspectives from the U.S. and Japan
overview: The increasing frequency and intensity of natural hazards associated with climate change, together with emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases, pose shared challenges for societies around the world. In recent years, research on crisis response has become increasingly diverse, expanding beyond field-based and practice-oriented studies to include new approaches using big data, artificial intelligence, and other emerging technologies. At the same time, the settings in which such research is conducted, as well as the social, cultural, and institutional contexts of the people and communities it seeks to understand, vary substantially across countries and cases.

Against this background, the workshop seeks to provide an overview of recent research trends in the United States and Japan while creating a space for dialogue across methodological and national contexts. By bringing together perspectives grounded in real-world practice, field-based research, and data- and technology-driven approaches, the workshop aims to explore how these different perspectives can complement one another and help identify shared research challenges and future directions for crisis response and societal resilience research.
goals: To provide an overview of recent research trends in crisis response and societal resilience in the United States and Japan.
To examine how differences in data, technologies, institutional arrangements, and social contexts shape the strengths and limitations of each country's approaches.
To identify shared research challenges and perspectives that can support the future development of crisis response and resilience research through cross-national and interdisciplinary dialogue.

featuredTalks.title: Disaster Digital Twin – Concept, Progress, and Application
featuredTalks.abstract: We demonstrate our research and practices of "Disaster Digital Twin (DDT)", a fusion of real-time simulation, mobile sensing, and multi-agent systems in cyberspace, to forecast damage, exposed populations, and optimized evacuation plans.
featuredTalks.speaker: Shunichi Koshimura
featuredTalks.affiliation: Director, International Research Institute of Disaster Science (IRIDeS), Tohoku University

featuredTalks.title: Human-Centered Mobile Sensing: Inferring Physical and Psychological States with Off-the-Shelf Mobile Devices
featuredTalks.abstract: This talk introduces a human-centered perspective on mobile sensing for understanding people's physical and psychological states using off-the-shelf mobile devices. Smartphones and wearable devices (e.g., smartwatches, smart rings, and earphones) have multimodal sensors (such as location, microphone, and motion sensors) and can capture various signals related to mobility, activity, location, proximity, and environmental context, offering new opportunities to infer human conditions in everyday life and during crises. I will discuss how such sensing technologies and their sensing framework can help detect behavioral changes, physical activity patterns, stress-related indicators, and potential vulnerabilities. The talk also highlights key challenges for real-world deployment, including privacy, data quality, interpretability, and responsible use of personal sensing data.
